newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end lower, except for palladium.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end lower, except for palladium.

text.p: COMEX and NYMEX precious metals futures ended lower Thursday, after a midsession recovery from early lows failed going into the close.
But nearby active palladium futures climbed to near contract highs as the physical platinum group metal (PGM) market tightened sharply again, led by new difficulties in the forward leasing market.
"There's a lot of uncertainty in the PGMs, but the lack of volume in gold and silver lately is keeping people away," said Andre DiMino, fund manager of Apostle Capital Management based in New Jersey.
"Many people are getting tired of waiting for gold to bounce, but the platinum/gold spread is proving profitable," he said.
"The funds are staying with currency plays for now, where liquidity is good and positions can be hedged. The metals will come back into their own, but gold may need another leg down first," he said.
COMEX August gold ended down $2.40 at $343.60 an ounce, returning to its session lows after an intraday recovery failed.

"We did some technical damage on the break of $345.00 overnight, with the U.S. dollar jumping, but a bounce ran into resistance again around $345.00 on the way back up intraday, prompting fund and trade selling at the close, leaving another test of the year's low around $340 likely basis spot in the bullion market," one trader said.
Overnight the August to April yen-based Tokyo gold futures surged by their 40-yen per gram daily limit as the yen fell against the dollar.
The U.S. dollar jumped above 115 yen after Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said Japan would act decisively against excessive moves in the currency market.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $341.30/80 an ounce, compared to the London Thursday afternoon fix at $342.20 and the New York close Wednesday around $343.60/10.
COMEX July silver closed down 3.7 cents at $4.780 an ounce, ahead of the expiry of July silver options Friday, with the focus on the $4.750 strike price, traders said.
Meanwhile, NYMEX July platinum ended down $10.70 at $433.10, as funds rolled out of the July contract and into the October delivery month.

But NYMEX September palladium went against the trend in the complex and ended up $5.75 at $184.25 an ounce, as uncertainty persisted about when Russian supplies would resume and what quantities the Russian would deliver.

Russian PGM exports have been suspended for five months, leading to an acute shortage of metal which is now beginning to hit consumers like automotive catalytic converter manufacturers and dental supply companies.
Many manufacturers have financed their supplies by leasing the metal in the forward market.

But the absence of Russian supplies has meant world inventories have been drawn down to the extent that some dental suppliers and glass manufacturers are now having difficulty rolling over their leases and are being forced to buy the metal in the spot market, sources said.
One month lease rates for both platinum and palladium rose back over 100 percent Thursday, while 12 month rates varied from 30 to 60 percent. Traditionally lease rates are less than five percent.

"If metal does not start coming back on line soon, if we don't start getting Russian material out, its going to have a very serious impact on our ability to make the product," one U.S. catalytic converter manufacturing source said.
Both platinum and palladium are used in the manufacture of catalytic converters which are used to reduce pollution in automobile exhaust systems worldwide.

"We're watching the lease rates, Norilsk (the Russian metal combine) is cranking the stuff out, and the Japanese remain confident their demand will be met, but waiting for the Russians is like 'Waiting for Godot'," one bullion banker said.
"Unlike Godot, hopefully the Russians will come."
Russian PGM exports are still expected to resume late June after annual supply contract talks broke down in December.
((Clive McKeef, New York Commodities Desk, 212-859-1641))
